speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He was living in the flat right above mine.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To me, he was the elder brother I never had.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We had always played together almost immediately after we returned from school.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He taught me how to ride the bicycle and we played chess together, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We went on many a cycling trip together, such as to the nearby beach at 15th mile, the cinema along Canberra Road or the public swimming pool at Deptford Road.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mani passed away around the early 1990s in a road traffic accident.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It was a double tragedy for the family as his pillion rider, his grandfather, died in the same accident, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a much higher figure, compared to the corresponding period in the previous two years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will discuss this worrying trend later in my speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Families of the victims of road accidents who die or suffer crippling injuries would also have to bear the pain and consequences of road traffic accidents permanently.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The unfortunate reality is that, every year, there are a significant number of road traffic fatalities and serious injuries here and elsewhere.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Globally, about 1.35 million people are killed on roads across the world every year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The number of serious injuries amounts to between 20 and 50 million annually.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Lives have intrinsic and economic value, both of which are lost in accidents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But it is not realistic to think about totally eradicating road accidents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a point that Lord Sumption, the famous former UK Law Lord, put across pithily in his Reith Lecture in 2019.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are, by far, the largest source of accidental, physical injury in this country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We could almost completely eliminate them by reviving the Locomotive Act of 1865 which limited the speed of motorised vehicles to four miles an hour in the country and two miles per hour in towns.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Today, we allow faster speeds than that, although we know for certain that it will mean many more people being killed or injured, and we do this because total safety would be too inconvenient.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, eliminating risk is not an absolute value, it is a question of degree." Sir, if it is a question of degree, then I think there is a case for Singapore to strive to achieve lower rates of fatalities and serious injuries arising from road accidents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore's roads are relatively safe when a comparison is done on a country-by-country basis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But the picture becomes a little different when we compare our RTF rates with several metropolitan cities in advanced countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Looking at its 2018-2022 figures, it has about 800,000 vehicles on its roads.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That translates to roughly about 200,000 less than ours for the same period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have slightly under one million vehicles on our roads.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hong Kong's resident population is, however, higher than ours at 7.4 million.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In comparison, our resident population is about two million smaller.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The average RTF rate per 100,000 population for Hong Kong for the period 2018-2022 is 1.43.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In comparison, ours is 1.92 for the same period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: London has more motor vehicles and a much bigger population.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 2022, London has 2.6 million registered vehicles.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 2022, 101 people were killed on London roads.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This leads to an RTF rate per 100,000 population of 1.15.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Tokyo's metropolitan area is amongst the most densely populated cities in the world with a population of 37 million as at 2022.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, it has only about three million vehicles comparatively.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The 2022 RTF rate for Tokyo was reported as 0.94 which is much lower than ours at 1.92 in 2022.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Man for man, Singapore loses more lives than Hong Kong, London and Tokyo.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We, however, compare favourably with cities, such as Seoul City, which had an RTF rate of 2.18, compared to our 1.46 in 2020, and New York, which had an RTF rate of 2.87, compared to our 1.92 in 2022.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I fully appreciate that the vehicle mix in each of the cities is different from Singapore's.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, the short point I am making is that, notwithstanding the limitations of my research, it is reasonable to infer that whilst we have done relatively well in terms of ensuring a high level of road safety on our roads, there remains room for improvement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As we all recognise, motorcyclists and pillion riders are amongst the most vulnerable road users.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I filed a Parliamentary Question (PQ) that came up for answer in May 2023 concerning fatalities amongst motorcyclists and pillion riders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The answers revealed that the fatality figure for the first quarter this year is double that of the corresponding figure in the same period for 2022 and 2021.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In an article in a Straits Times dated 7 May 2023, Mr Bernard Tay, Chairman of the Singapore Road Safety Council, was reported as saying, "The figure is alarming, but it needs to be analysed further to understand the number better." I fully agree with Mr Tay's suggestion and would respectfully commend it to the Government for its consideration.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Anecdotally, I have received feedback from my residents in Bukit Batok on the matter, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Hairul, aged 32, is an Auxiliary Police Officer who is deployed at Changi Prison Complex.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He travels to and fro his workplace via motorcycle.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He told me he has noticed an uptick of motorcyclists weaving in and out of traffic at great speed and without signalling early.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He also noticed a higher number of drivers who are using their mobile phones while driving and not being conscious of blind spots when making turns.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There are many amongst us who are concerned about the safety of delivery motorcycle riders who have a high cognitive tax on them each day on the road, including the need to look at mobile phone apps and the stresses from wanting to make as many delivery trips as possible.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Police, in its statement, stated that the causes for the uptick include motorcyclists failing to maintain a proper control of their bikes, not keeping a proper lookout and disobeying traffic light signals.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do appreciate that the Government has already been taking active steps to enhance road safety over the years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For instance, just within a space of three years between 2019 and 2021, the Road Traffic Act was amended twice with a suite of measures, including the enhancing of criminal sanctions, to deter irresponsible driving and improve road safety.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These amendments received broad support from hon Members of this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To my knowledge, Traffic Police has been actively enforcing these provisions against offending motorists, especially against those who are caught speeding and beating red lights.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are often cited as the top two reasons for accidents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The officers of Traffic Police deserve our full support in their enforcement efforts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister for Home Affairs, in answer to my PQ, also highlighted that the Traffic Police, the Land Transport Authority (LTA) and the Singapore Road Safety Council have implemented various initiatives to strengthen road safety awareness amongst road users.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Indeed, the Minister's three-pronged approach of making our roads safer through education, engagement and enforcement has much to commend for itself.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: LTA has also taken several important steps to make our roads safer for us.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: LTA also has other initiatives, such as setting up Silver Zones, appropriate road markings, lighted road studs, integrated pedestrian countdown timers and signs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All these moves, cumulatively, are in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Notwithstanding, I believe there is scope for greater room for the use of technology to compensate for human error and inattention.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to harness safety technology to move the needle more aggressively so as to reduce death and serious injuries on our roads.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Over the years, there have been great strides taken in technological developments to improve the safety features found in vehicles.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Beyond the standard seatbelts, airbags and Anti-lock Braking System (ABS), we now have access to safety technology in the form of blind-spot warning systems; rear cross traffic alerts; automatic emergency braking and pedestrian detection systems; lane keep assists; and adaptive cruise controls.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would add that these technologies are not new technologies that would have to be test-bedded to check for reliability.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These technologies have long reached a steady state.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Do these crash avoidance technologies result in fewer collisions and save lives?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Based on my research, the answer is yes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The crash prevention costs savings, according to the same article, if the technologies were mandated throughout the light-duty vehicle fleet, based on certain assumptions, would be up to US$264 billion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Europe, they have gone one step further.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With respect to safety features in motorcycles, it seemed to me that, whilst there are a number of safety features that have been implemented arising from technological advances, they are not as widely adopted as compared to motor vehicles.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They include ABS for motorcycles; combined braking systems to engage front and rear brakes at the same time; and traction and stability controls.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In March 2023, the European Transport Safety Council called on EU countries to introduce ABS for all motorcycles, including those under 125 cubic centimetres (cc).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Whether its recommendation will be implemented though is not certain.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Calls have been made in several countries, including Malaysia, to introduce speed limiters on motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is the downside to mandating the use of safety technology in our vehicles?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We need to balance this against costs savings arising from crash prevention, as I highlighted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, we cannot put a price to the saving of lives and avoiding of crippling injuries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, I noted in a 2020 article issued by McKinsey & Company that when regulators make safety features mandatory, like in the case in Europe, the market will react to make these features commoditised over time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If that is indeed the case, the costs will, over time, moderate downwards.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, 37.2% of cars on Singapore roads were registered within the past five years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I, therefore, anticipate that a good number of these vehicles would already be installed with important safety features that l spoke about earlier as standard fare.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The cost consequences should these safety features be mandated may not be as significant, as what would be more likely to happen is a standardisation of technologies amongst the cars.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may not be so for buses though.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, I acknowledge that the cost consequence of making it mandatory for these heavy vehicles to carry mandated safety features may be higher.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With respect, I think our regulations mandating safety features in vehicles are somewhat behind the curve.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have, in my opinion, only a small raft of regulations mandating use of safety technologies in our vehicles.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have regulations mandating the use of seat belts, for example.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They will add slightly to the cost and we can take an incremental approach to their introduction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But overall, I think it is a small price to pay to reduce the number of deaths and serious injuries on our roads.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Borrowing the words from Emily Dickenson's poem, "My friend Mani did not want to stop for Death, but Death, unkindly, stopped for him." There can be far fewer such hard stops if we all resolve to improve the safety requirements for all our modern-day carriages, be they bikes, cars, buses or lorries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As road users, I am certain Members in this House would be able to relate to the issues raised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Our goal is to have safer roads for all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is an ongoing journey that requires collective effort from every road user.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Member has rightly pointed out that technology can be an enabler for improving road safety outcomes in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Traffic Police (TP) has also made it mandatory for such vehicles to install speed limiters, as the Member has said.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For vehicles, apart from motorcycles, LTA has allowed the use of camera monitor systems in lieu of conventional rear-view mirrors from 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For public buses, they have progressively been fitted with safety features, such as the Driver Anti-Fatigue System to monitor the bus captain's fatigue level and the Collision Warning System to alert the bus captain on impending collisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: And while the measures target larger vehicles, they also protect other road users, such as motorcyclists, cyclists and pedestrians.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Technology can only be implemented effectively after careful consideration of other factors, such as road design and user behaviour, as well as extensive industry engagement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For each change, many factors have to be assessed, including motorists' readiness to adapt to the new technology, the reliability of the new technology, cost effectiveness, as well as the impact on motorist behaviour with the adoption of new technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These considerations apply to safety technology on all types of vehicles, including motorcycles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In the case of motorcycles, advanced braking systems, such as Combined Braking System (CBS) and Anti-lock Braking System (ABS) that the Member mentioned in his speech, have increasingly been made available on smaller and larger engine capacity motorcycles respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: LTA is aware of campaigns overseas to mandate ABS for all motorcycles, regardless of engine capacity and is studying the impact if we were to impose such requirements locally, based on the factors I cited earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Besides vehicle technology, there are three other pillars in our ecosystem to improve road safety.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These are road design, user behaviour and regulations and enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: First, at the very core of road safety is road design.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is an iterative and ongoing effort by LTA as it regularly reviews traffic accident data to identify areas with higher accident rates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For these identified areas, LTA will conduct detailed investigations to assess the need for additional road safety measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Where necessary, road improvements, such as traffic calming measures and signages, as well as road safety barriers, are introduced.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: It takes into account the demographic changes of nearby communities and incorporates the needs of the residents and stakeholders it serves.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Members of this House would likely be familiar with Silver and School Zones, which serve to provide safer roads for our seniors and students in areas where these vulnerable groups are in higher proportion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Apart from implementing traffic calming measures, LTA implements a lower road speed limit of 40 kilometres per hour or 30 kilometres per hour in Silver Zones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will continue to build on these efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: At this year's Committee of Supply debate, I introduced the concept of Friendly Streets and announced that we will be piloting Friendly Streets at five locations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is an ambitious and meaningful endeavour, as we move from making specific zones safer, to making entire streets more pedestrian-friendly and we are doing so in two ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: First, by changing the road infrastructure with various moves, such as road pinching, more crossings, lower speed limits, to make these roads safer for pedestrians.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Second, by bringing in the local community to give us feedback and work with us to make these roads more conducive and safer, not just for travel, but also for other daily activities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We want safer streets and safer journeys for all road users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But our goal is to improve road safety and that will not be complete without the software, which is road user behaviour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To have safer and more gracious roads, we will need to have safer and more gracious behaviour by all road users, which include motorists, cyclists and pedestrians alike.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: TP works closely with the Singapore Road Safety Council to continually improve safety on our roads by inculcating good safety practices among all road users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: TP also conducts weekly engagements with various groups and stakeholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In addition, TP leverages on technology, such as launching the compulsory simulator training since 2019 for new drivers to experience the top causes of accidents and practise defensive driving under a safe and controlled environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This allows them to appreciate the dangers on the roads and be more situationally aware of blind spots when driving on the roads.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We could have the safest road designs and the best technology in our vehicles.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: But it is considerate, caring and gracious behaviour by all while using our roads that will improve our daily commutes and make them safer for everyone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: A third and critical component to improving our road safety is road regulations and enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These are the traffic laws and rules that all road users must obey to ensure safe roads for all to use.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: And this is the basic framework and tenet to encourage compliance and deter misconduct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Of course, enforcement plays an important role in ensuring compliance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Enforcement takes place through the deployment of resources on the ground and with the use of technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Besides the deployment of officers to conduct daily and targeted enforcement, TP adopts new technology to augment its enforcement efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For instance, mobile speed cameras were deployed to increase versatility of traffic enforcements at new locations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I appreciate the Member’s suggestion and thank him once again for raising this Adjournment Motion.
